text: Big Brother 2000, retroactively known as Big Brother 1 following season 7, was the debut season of the American reality television series Big Brother, which was based on the Dutch series of the same name that gained popularity in 1999 and 2000. The season premiered on July 5, 2000, and lasted for 88 days, concluding with Eddie McGee as the winner and Josh Souza as the runner-up. The format differed significantly from later seasons, as ten strangers lived in a custom-built house with no contact with the outside world, including no phone, television, internet, magazines, newspapers, or communication with those outside the house—except in cases of family emergencies or deaths. The HouseGuests were constantly filmed and not allowed to communicate with the filmmakers. Every other week, each HouseGuest nominated two others, and the two with the most nominations were marked for banishment; viewers then voted to decide which nominee left during a live show. When only three HouseGuests remained, the public voted to determine the winner of the $500,000 grand prize, with the runner-up receiving $100,000 and the second runner-up receiving $50,000. HouseGuests completed weekly tasks, wagering a portion of their weekly shopping budget—either winning double or losing their wager depending on performance—and were required to work as a team. If food ran out, an emergency ration was available. They also visited the Red Room to share thoughts and feelings. The series was structured as a social experiment, emphasizing interactions among individuals with differing beliefs and backgrounds, as noted by Nina Tassler of CBS. HouseGuests could quit the game but would not be allowed back into the house, and breaking rules could result in expulsion. The first season featured ten HouseGuests: Brittany, Cassandra, Curtis, Eddie, Karen, George, Jamie, Jordan, Josh, and William. On Day 1, they began with a word puzzle to find grocery money, earning $100. On Day 3, they built a clock from potatoes, passing the task. On Day 4, they made plaster masks. On Day 5, a chicken was injured and later returned. On Day 7, they attempted to recall whether celebrities were alive or dead, failing and wagering 20% of their budget; William intentionally failed, upsetting others. On Day 9, William and Jordan were nominated, with William receiving six and Jordan five nominations. On Day 17, William was banished after receiving 73% of the public vote. On Day 20, they built 12,100 dominoes to fall in a single knock, passing the task and wagering 20%; they also held a fake trial with Karen as judge, Jordan on trial, Brittany as witness, Curtis and Cassandra as lawyers, and others as jurors. On Day 22, Curtis and Jordan were nominated, with Curtis receiving six and Jordan five nominations; Josh, Jamie, Cassandra, and Brittany received none. On Day 28, they held a roast for Curtis and Jordan, who were then banished on Day 30 when Jordan received 78% of the public vote. On Day 36, George was voted to receive a phone call from home. That night, Cassandra, Josh, and Karen were marked for banishment due to a tie, with George receiving no nominations. They were given a task to care for a pug named Chiquita. Karen began asking viewers to banish her due to missing her children. On Day 44, they held a live challenge where they were offered a reward for watching nominations but declined. On Day 44, Karen was banished after receiving 76% of the public vote. On Day 49, they memorized major U.S. highways, passing the task and wagering 20%; they later painted each other like animals. In a sumo wrestling competition, Eddie won a luxury massage, with William secretly giving him a bad one. They had two HouseGuests dancing at all times, passing the task and wagering 20%. On Day 50, due to a tie, Brittany, Cassandra, Curtis, Eddie, George, and Josh were marked for banishment—making it the first time all HouseGuests received at least one nomination. Jamie won a two-minute conversation with a casting director. They named "Mr. and Miss Big Brother 2000" with Eddie, Brittany, and Cassandra winning a dinner. On Day 58, Jamie co-hosted an episode with Julie Chen and announced the banishment. On Day 58, Brittany was banished after receiving 34% of the public vote. On Day 64, Cassandra, Curtis, and Eddie were marked for banishment. All HouseGuests received at least one nomination. The remaining six were offered $20,000 to leave, later increased to $50,000, with Beth Thieme set to enter if someone accepted; none accepted, so Beth did not join. That night, Brittany and Josh completed a task. They estimated the price of a luxury item, earning it if within one dollar. They trained Chiquita for an obstacle course, passing the task and wagering 20%. Curtis won a reward to attend the 52nd Primetime Emmy Awards. On Day 72, they wrote a message to be flown on a banner plane. On Day 72, Cassandra was banished after receiving 46% of the public vote. On Day 74, they had five minutes to make a phone call to a loved one. On Day 74, they made live nominations, marking Curtis, Eddie, George, and Jamie for banishment; Josh received no nominations. They wrote lyrics for the show’s theme song and recorded it in the Red Room. Josh won a task to find Chiquita and present the weather. On Day 79, the five remaining HouseGuests selected Cassandra to return. On Day 79, George was banished after receiving 51% of the public vote. On Day 81, due to a tie, all four remaining HouseGuests were marked for banishment—this was the final round of nominations. Former HouseGuest Cassandra entered the house as a guest. Josh was selected as a saboteur, tasked with setting the potato clock back; Curtis correctly guessed and won a flat-screen television. On Day 86, Jamie was banished after receiving 31% of the public vote. Chiquita exited and was adopted by a couple. On Day 88, Curtis was banished after receiving 14% of the public vote. Minutes later, Josh received 27% of the public vote, placing second, while Eddie won with 59% of the public vote. The Big Brother series first launched in the Netherlands, with editions in countries like Germany achieving public popularity. Following its international success, a bidding war occurred among CBS, ABC, and a cable network for the rights to the show, with the series initially planned to last 100 days. Mark Itkin of William Morris noted the intense bidding, citing the show’s unique elements, including its 100-day run and Internet component, as particularly appealing to networks. CBS ultimately secured the rights for an estimated $20 million, with production costs later reported at $200,000 per episode. Paul Romer, co-creator of the original series, served as Executive Producer and emphasized that the show centers on human emotions such as love, hate, fighting, crying, and laughing. Romer clarified that the show is not primarily about sexual content or nudity. The series was one of the first reality shows to air and required a crew of over 150 people. The first season featured Julie Chen as the main host and Ian O'Malley as co-host; O'Malley, who initially expressed uncertainty about the show and noted the impact of the SAG strike, was released after one month and later cited the buyout as a relief. Chen, who initially declined the hosting role due to concerns about being placed in the entertainment division, was pressured by CBS News president Andrew Heyward, who warned that refusal could be seen as insubordination. Dr. Drew Pinsky and Regina Lewis appeared weekly to discuss house events. The cast included HouseGuest William, a member of the New Black Panther Party, Jamie, who was Miss Washington USA the year before joining, Curtis and Josh, who had prior modeling experience, Jean Jordan, a former exotic dancer, and Karen and George, who were married with children; Cassandra and William were both African-American. Creator John de Mol stated that the 10 houseguests were ordinary people relatable to viewers, and that the show demonstrated that ordinary individuals could be interesting. The first season premiered on July 5, 2000, with a filmed premiere on July 4, 2000, and aired five nights per week, later expanding to six episodes weekly, which shifted the live banishment episode to Wednesday. Four episodes were half-hour daily recaps, one was an hourly weekly recap, and the sixth was the live banishment, during which a HouseGuest was interviewed by Julie Chen. The season totaled 70 episodes, the most for any season, and lasted 88 days. The theme song, "Live," performed by Jonathan Clarke, played during closing credits and throughout the show. Viewers could watch live feeds on the official website, which were edited for music rights and privacy, and included a disclaimer for users under 21. The house was a one-story, 1,800-square-foot facility at the CBS Studio Center in Los Angeles, featuring two bedrooms, a kitchen, dining room, and one bathroom, with 28 cameras and 60 microphones, requiring HouseGuests to wear microphones at all times. Walls included two-way mirrors with behind-the-scenes filming, and bedrooms had infrared cameras for dark room coverage. The house had bad feng shui, clashing colors, and bright themes, with the kitchen in blue and living room in yellow; both bedrooms were identical with bunk and single beds, and the bathroom had one toilet, shower, washboard, and washtub. The Red Room was used for sharing thoughts and completing tasks, and the backyard had a patio and chicken coop, with HouseGuests able to use the eggs as food. Big Brother 1 premiered with over 22 million viewers, but ratings quickly declined, dropping out of the Top 10, with a notable drop after the banishments of Will "Mega" and Jordan. The show reached its highest ratings on Wednesdays, following Survivor: Borneo, but saw lower viewership on July 8, when it was beaten by Cops. Ratings continued to fall, with one episode reaching only 5.5 million viewers, though Cassandra’s banishment episode drew 12.5 million, and the finale attracted 11.13 million, surpassing the Olympics. Despite declining ratings, the official website saw high traffic due to the live feed, which increased in usage as ratings dropped, and the online aspect was credited with changing the show’s dynamic and content, making it one of the most popular new websites in July. Critics and fans often described the series as "boring," with John Carman of The San Francisco Chronicle calling the show’s focus on trivial details like Kleenex usage uninteresting, and comedian Kathy Griffin mocking the show as featuring "tards." Joyce Millman of Salon.com attributed the drop in ratings to the "boring" cast, and the New York Times reported CBS’s disappointment. Les Moonves, CBS chief, criticized the casting and noted that more provocative storylines were dropped. John de Mol blamed both the casting and format changes to suit American audiences, while Paul Romer believed the HouseGuests were overly conscious of the cameras and concerned about their on-screen image. Former co-host Ian O'Malley predicted the show would be panned, citing the voyeuristic nature. The series faced controversy upon announcement, including a lawsuit by Chicago attorney Marvin Rosenblum, who claimed CBS and Orwell Productions illegally used the "Big Brother" name from George Orwell’s novel Nineteen Eighty-Four and deceived the public. The lawsuit was denied in January 2001 and settled under undisclosed terms. Controversy also arose over Chen’s hosting role, with Andy Rooney of 60 Minutes criticizing her involvement as a deterioration of news standards, and concerns raised about scripted lines. Security was breached when two screenwriters threw a tennis ball with fake news stories—such as a claim that President Bill Clinton called Big Brother a "national disgrace"—into the garden, and a plane flew a banner reading "Big Brother is worse than you think. Get out now." George Boswell’s wife and family campaigned for viewers to vote out popular HouseGuests to keep George in the game, which Brittany informed Josh about, leading to anti-George banners being flown over the house. HouseGuests often felt misrepresented and were required to perform unwanted acts. George attempted to leave the game during a live episode, but none of the HouseGuests chose to exit. There was speculation that CBS orchestrated the banners, though it was never confirmed. Despite poor ratings and controversies, Big Brother helped CBS achieve a 17% increase in its time slot and was renewed in September 2000 for a second season, with numerous format changes confirmed.
